demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette: After six sessions, I can no longer separate Elias from the landscape that shaped him and the afternoon that fractured it. At 54, he sits in the chair across from me with a stillness that reads as control, but his body remembers what his mind has filed away. His story moves through time in straight, deliberate lines, yet his nervous system remains stuck on a single switchback trail three years ago. The wind was carrying a hard rain when he first guided his chainsaw into the trunk of a mature western red cedar. He was working a timber harvest, the way he had for two decades, reading slope and lean the way others read weather. His boot caught on a slick mat of pine needles. He stepped back, raised the safety pole, and the tree listed wrong. It swung faster than gravity should allow, striking a young surveyor who had been marking the clearance zone. The sound is not what Elias focuses on; it is the sudden collapse of the man's posture, the wet tear of fabric, the abrupt silence that follows metal meeting bone. Elias fell to his knees, pressing his bare hands against the gash, whispering that he was sorry, that he would hold him there until the medics came. The surveyor survived, but lost the lower leg. The incident report cleared Elias of negligence, but the words sit in his chest like wet gravel. He quit the line of work for a season. He could not stand the idle hum of an engine, could not walk past a hardware store without his throat tightening. His wife, Clara, found him on the back porch at 3 a.m., staring at the tree line, fingers trembling as he traced the phantom weight of a chainsaw handle. Sleep abandoned him. When he finally drifted off, the dark was populated by the angle of falling timber, the scuff of safety boots, the terrible sound of impact. He began checking the deadbolt four times. He stopped driving on gravel roads. When Clara reached for him in bed, his spine went rigid, his breath catching until he forced himself to blink and remember who lay beside him. Now, Elias consults on trail stabilization and erosion control for the county, sitting at a folding table in a sunlit office surrounded by topographic maps and satellite imagery. He prefers the quiet. He prefers the predictability of contour lines. But the forest outside his window still makes his pulse jump. Last Tuesday, a large branch cracked in a gust, and he dropped his coffee mug, shattering it across the linoleum, his heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird. He spent the next hour sitting on the bathroom floor, running cold water over his wrists, waiting for the tremors to subside. He tells himself it is just stress, just age, but the explanation feels thin. He avoids orange safety vests. The sight triggers a tightness in his chest that makes it hard to draw a full breath. He watches his own hands constantly now, turning them over, flexing his fingers as if checking for damage that isn't there. He flinches when car doors slam. He measures his wife's footsteps when she walks down the hall, counting the seconds it takes for them to reach the kitchen, needing to know she is moving at a safe, predictable pace. He loves her, fiercely, but he keeps the center of the bed like a trench. He watches her sleep, afraid that if he closes his eyes, the tree will fall again. He wakes before dawn every morning, staring at the ceiling, replaying the switchback trail in his head, wondering if he could have turned his boot a half-inch sooner, if he could have gripped the pole a second harder, if he could have rewound the afternoon just enough to change the outcome. He does not speak of it at work. He does not speak of it at home. He just waits for the day the fear stops tasting like iron.
